24	// Webhooks: telling something else that a brain changed.
25	//
26	// What a brain learns stays inside it until somebody runs a command. That is
27	// fine for a tool you sit in front of and useless for everything downstream — a
28	// CI job that should re-run when an invariant is recorded, a channel that should
29	// see a decision, an index that needs rebuilding. Nothing could subscribe.
30	//
31	// It is also outbound network traffic from a product whose default build makes
32	// none, so the rules are strict and configuration cannot loosen them:
33	//
34	//   - Off unless ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL is set. No config file, no discovery,
35	//     no default endpoint. A URL has to be typed.
36	//   - brainNoEgressMode() wins. ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS silences
37	//     webhooks even with a URL configured, and the check happens here rather
38	//     than at each call site. A local-only promise one subsystem can opt out of
39	//     is not a promise.
40	//   - Fact text is withheld unless ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT says
41	//     otherwise, and that decision is made in newFactWebhookEvent so no caller
42	//     can forget it. The default payload is ids, kinds and taxonomy paths:
43	//     enough to trigger work, not enough to turn one env var into a feed of
44	//     everything the brain knows.
45	//   - Redirects are refused rather than followed. A webhook POST carries the
46	//     payload and its signature; following a 307 to somewhere else delivers
47	//     both to a host nobody configured. An endpoint that redirects is a
48	//     misconfiguration and is reported as one.
49	//   - Delivery never fails the command that triggered it. Recording a fact
50	//     succeeds or fails on its own terms; an unreachable endpoint is a warning
51	//     on stderr. The alternative is a brain that cannot write anything because
52	//     something unrelated is down.
53	
54	const (
55		webhookURLEnv         = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL"
56		webhookSecretEnv      = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET"
57		webhookIncludeTextEnv = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT"
58		webhookTimeoutEnv     = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT"
59	
60		// Delivery is synchronous and therefore on the critical path of every
61		// command that triggers it, so this is a latency budget rather than a
62		// generous ceiling. Two seconds is long enough for a local or same-region
63		// receiver and short enough that an unresponsive one does not make
64		// `remember` feel broken — it is called by agents, often.
65		//
66		// It cannot be made asynchronous by moving it to a goroutine: these are
67		// short-lived CLI processes, and a detached send is killed when the command
68		// returns, which is not "fire and forget" but "usually do not fire".
69		defaultWebhookTimeout = 2 * time.Second

72	// webhookTimeout is the per-delivery deadline, overridable for a receiver that
73	// is legitimately slow.
74	func webhookTimeout() time.Duration {
75		raw := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookTimeoutEnv))
76		if raw == "" {
77			return defaultWebhookTimeout
78		}
79		parsed, err := time.ParseDuration(raw)
80		if err != nil || parsed <= 0 {
81			tui.Warnf(os.Stderr, "%s is not a positive duration; using %s", webhookTimeoutEnv, defaultWebhookTimeout)
82			return defaultWebhookTimeout
83		}
84		return parsed
85	}

87	// The events that exist. Every name here is emitted by real code in this
88	// package; the list is deliberately not padded with events a consumer could
89	// subscribe to and never receive.
90	const (
91		WebhookFactRecorded   = "fact.recorded"
92		WebhookFactRetracted  = "fact.retracted"
93		WebhookBrainRefreshed = "brain.refreshed"
94		WebhookTest           = "webhook.test"

97	// webhookCatalogue is the single list of what this brain sends and what each
98	// event means. `webhook events` prints it and the README quotes it, so neither
99	// can drift from the code; and because the descriptions live here rather than
100	// beside the command, a constant's only mention outside this file is a real
101	// emission — which is what TestEveryAdvertisedEventIsActuallyEmitted checks.
102	func webhookCatalogue() []struct{ Name, Description string } {
103		return []struct{ Name, Description string }{
104			{WebhookFactRecorded, "a durable fact was recorded (`remember`)"},
105			{WebhookFactRetracted, "a fact was marked no longer true (`facts retract`)"},
106			{WebhookBrainRefreshed, "the brain finished a refresh"},
107			{WebhookTest, "sent only by `webhook test`"},
108		}
109	}

111	func webhookEventNames() []string {
112		names := make([]string, 0, 4)
113		for _, event := range webhookCatalogue() {
114			names = append(names, event.Name)

116		return names

119	type webhookFact struct {
120		ID    string   `json:"id"`
121		Kind  string   `json:"kind,omitempty"`
122		Paths []string `json:"paths,omitempty"`
123		// Text is present only when ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT is set.
124		Text string `json:"text,omitempty"`
125	}
126	
127	type webhookEvent struct {
128		Event     string         `json:"event"`
129		Timestamp string         `json:"timestamp"`
130		Repo      string         `json:"repo,omitempty"`
131		Branch    string         `json:"branch,omitempty"`
132		Global    bool           `json:"global,omitempty"`
133		Fact      *webhookFact   `json:"fact,omitempty"`
134		Counts    map[string]int `json:"counts,omitempty"`
135	}

137	// webhookRepoName is the repository's directory name, not its path. A consumer
138	// needs to tell two repos apart; it does not need to learn the layout of
139	// somebody's home directory.
140	func webhookRepoName(repoDir string) string {
141		repoDir = strings.TrimSpace(repoDir)
142		if repoDir == "" {
143			return ""
144		}
145		return filepath.Base(filepath.Clean(repoDir))
146	}
147	
148	// webhookRepoIdentity resolves the name every event for one repository reports.
149	//
150	// It must be one source for all of them. Call sites had drifted between the
151	// git-toplevel path and the configured repo root, which differ whenever a
152	// repository is reached through a symlink or from a subdirectory — so
153	// fact.recorded and fact.retracted could name the same physical repository
154	// differently, and a subscriber correlating by `repo` would see two.
155	//
156	// The git toplevel is the one that is stable under both, and it falls back to
157	// the configured root when git cannot answer.
158	func webhookRepoIdentity(ctx context.Context, opts Options) string {
159		if top, err := base.GitScalar(ctx, opts.Runner, opts.Env.RepoRoot, "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"); err == nil {
160			if name := webhookRepoName(strings.TrimSpace(top)); name != "" {
161				return name
162			}
163		}
164		return webhookRepoName(opts.Env.RepoRoot)
165	}
166	
167	// newFactWebhookEvent builds a fact event and is the ONLY place that decides
168	// whether fact text leaves the machine. Callers pass the whole record and get
169	// back a payload already redacted, so forgetting to redact is not something a
170	// call site can do.
171	func newFactWebhookEvent(name, repoName, branch string, record factRecord, now time.Time) webhookEvent {
172		fact := &webhookFact{ID: record.ID, Kind: record.Kind, Paths: record.Paths}
173		if base.EnvBool(webhookIncludeTextEnv) {
174			fact.Text = record.Text
175		}
176		return webhookEvent{
177			Event:     name,
178			Timestamp: now.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
179			Repo:      repoName,
180			Branch:    branch,
181			Fact:      fact,
182		}
183	}
184	
185	// webhookEndpoint resolves the configured endpoint, and explains itself when
186	// there is none — `webhook status` prints the reason, so a webhook that is off
187	// because of a typo is distinguishable from one that was never configured.
188	func webhookEndpoint() (endpoint string, ok bool, reason string) {
189		if base.BrainNoEgressMode() {
190			return "", false, "egress is disabled by " + base.NoEgressToggleName()
191		}
192		raw := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookURLEnv))
193		if raw == "" {
194			return "", false, webhookURLEnv + " is not set"
195		}
196		parsed, err := url.Parse(raw)
197		if err != nil {
198			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s is not a valid URL", webhookURLEnv)
199		}
200		// Scheme before host, deliberately: file:///tmp/x parses with an empty host,
201		// so checking the host first reports it as a malformed URL when the real
202		// objection — and the one the user needs to read — is the scheme.
203		// No filtering of loopback, link-local or private addresses, deliberately.
204		//
205		// SSRF is a confused-deputy problem: it matters when an attacker supplies a
206		// URL that a MORE privileged component fetches. This URL has exactly one
207		// source — an environment variable the operator sets — and no config file,
208		// discovery or remote input can reach it. Anyone who can set it already
209		// runs code as that user and does not need a webhook to reach the network.
210		//
211		// Blocking loopback would also break the primary local use: a receiver on
212		// 127.0.0.1 is the obvious way to consume these on a machine that is the
213		// point of a local-first tool.
214		//
215		// What would change this: if the endpoint ever became settable from a
216		// config file, a repository-local file, or anything a second party can
217		// write, it stops being operator input and the address filtering belongs
218		// back on the list.
219		if parsed.Scheme != "http" && parsed.Scheme != "https" {
220			// A file:// or unix:// "webhook" is not a webhook, and admitting one
221			// turns an environment variable into a write primitive.
222			scheme := parsed.Scheme
223			if scheme == "" {
224				scheme = "no scheme"
225			}
226			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s must be http or https, not %s", webhookURLEnv, scheme)
227		}
228		if parsed.Host == "" {
229			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s has no host", webhookURLEnv)
230		}
231		return raw, true, ""
232	}
233	
234	// signWebhook returns the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the body, or "" when no secret is
235	// configured. Without it a receiver cannot tell a notification from this brain
236	// apart from a POST by anything else that learned the URL.
237	func signWebhook(body []byte) string {
238		secret := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookSecretEnv))
239		if secret == "" {
240			return ""
241		}
242		mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(secret))
243		mac.Write(body)
244		return hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
245	}
246	
247	// redactWebhookURL removes the endpoint from a transport error.
248	//
249	// For many receivers the URL IS the credential — a Slack or Discord incoming
250	// webhook is a secret path, and plenty of others carry a token in the query.
251	// http.Client.Do returns a *url.Error whose message embeds the whole thing, and
252	// this error is printed to stderr on every transient failure: into CI logs,
253	// agent transcripts and error monitoring. The host is enough to diagnose a
254	// delivery problem; the rest is a secret with no reason to be in a log.
255	func redactWebhookURL(err error) error {
256		var urlErr *url.Error
257		if !errors.As(err, &urlErr) {
258			return err
259		}
260		host := "the configured endpoint"
261		if parsed, parseErr := url.Parse(urlErr.URL); parseErr == nil && parsed.Host != "" {
262			host = parsed.Scheme + "://" + parsed.Host
263		}
264		// Rebuilt rather than string-replaced: the unwrapped cause carries the
265		// reason (timeout, connection refused, TLS failure) and does not contain
266		// the URL, so this keeps everything diagnostic and drops only the secret.
267		return fmt.Errorf("%s %s: %w", urlErr.Op, host, urlErr.Unwrap())
268	}
269	
270	// errWebhookRedirect is returned rather than followed. See the header comment:
271	// the payload and its signature must not be delivered to a host the user did
272	// not configure.
273	var errWebhookRedirect = errors.New("webhook endpoint redirected; point " + webhookURLEnv + " at the final URL instead")
274	
275	// Two bounds, deliberately: the client timeout covers the request and the
276	// context covers the whole operation. They are mutually redundant today —
277	// removing either alone leaves the other enforcing — so the test asserts the
278	// property (a stalled endpoint costs about the timeout and no more) rather than
279	// either mechanism. Removing both turns it red.
280	func newWebhookClient() *http.Client {
281		return &http.Client{
282			Timeout: webhookTimeout(),
283			CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
284				return errWebhookRedirect
285			},
286		}
287	}
288	
289	// emitWebhook delivers one event, or does nothing when webhooks are off. It
290	// returns an error so tests and `webhook test` can assert on delivery; the
291	// write paths use notifyWebhook instead and do not fail on it.
292	func emitWebhook(ctx context.Context, event webhookEvent) error {
293		endpoint, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint()
294		if !ok {
295			return nil // not configured is the normal case, not a failure
296		}
297		return deliverWebhook(ctx, endpoint, event)
298	}
299	
300	func deliverWebhook(ctx context.Context, endpoint string, event webhookEvent) error {
301		body, err := json.Marshal(event)
302		if err != nil {
303			return fmt.Errorf("encode webhook: %w", err)
304		}
305		if ctx == nil {
306			ctx = context.Background()
307		}
308		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, webhookTimeout())
309		defer cancel()
310	
311		request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
312		if err != nil {
313			return fmt.Errorf("build webhook request: %w", err)
314		}
315		request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
316		request.Header.Set("User-Agent", "entire-brain")
317		request.Header.Set("X-Entire-Event", event.Event)
318		if signature := signWebhook(body); signature != "" {
319			request.Header.Set("X-Entire-Signature-256", "sha256="+signature)
320		}
321	
322		response, err := newWebhookClient().Do(request)
323		if err != nil {
324			if errors.Is(err, errWebhookRedirect) {
325				return errWebhookRedirect
326			}
327			return fmt.Errorf("deliver webhook: %w", redactWebhookURL(err))
328		}
329		defer func() {
330			_, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4<<10))
331			_ = response.Body.Close()
332		}()
333		if response.StatusCode >= 400 {
334			return fmt.Errorf("webhook endpoint returned %s", response.Status)
335		}
336		return nil
337	}
338	
339	// notifyFactWebhook is what the fact write paths call.
340	//
341	// It checks whether webhooks are on BEFORE resolving anything, because
342	// resolving the repository identity shells out to git. Building the event
343	// eagerly and letting emitWebhook discard it put a subprocess on every
344	// `remember` and every `facts retract` for people who have never configured a
345	// webhook — which is the opposite of the promise that an unconfigured webhook
346	// costs nothing, on a path the rest of this file notes is called by agents,
347	// often.
348	func notifyFactWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, opts Options, event, branch string, record factRecord, now time.Time) {
349		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
350			return
351		}
352		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, newFactWebhookEvent(event, webhookRepoIdentity(ctx, opts), branch, record, now))
353	}
354	
355	// Global mutations belong to no repository, including the current checkout.
356	// Keep the same redaction and delivery policy without resolving a repo identity.
357	func notifyGlobalFactWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, event string, record factRecord, now time.Time) {
358		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
359			return
360		}
361		payload := newFactWebhookEvent(event, "", "", record, now)
362		payload.Global = true
363		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, payload)
364	}
365	
366	// notifyBrainWebhook is the same short-circuit for events that carry no fact.
367	func notifyBrainWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, opts Options, event string, now time.Time) {
368		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
369			return
370		}
371		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, webhookEvent{
372			Event:     event,
373			Timestamp: now.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
374			Repo:      webhookRepoIdentity(ctx, opts),
375		})
376	}
377	
378	// notifyWebhook is what the write paths call. It never returns an error,
379	// because no fact should fail to be recorded over a webhook — but it does
380	// block, for up to the timeout, and calling it "fire and forget" was wrong.
381	// A slow endpoint slows the command; ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT is how that
382	// is bounded.
383	func notifyWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, event webhookEvent) {
384		if err := emitWebhook(ctx, event); err != nil && errOut != nil {
385			fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "warning: webhook %s not delivered: %v\n", event.Event, err)
386		}
387	}

22	)
23	
24	// Webhooks: telling something else that a brain changed.
25	//
26	// What a brain learns stays inside it until somebody runs a command. That is
27	// fine for a tool you sit in front of and useless for everything downstream — a
28	// CI job that should re-run when an invariant is recorded, a channel that should
29	// see a decision, an index that needs rebuilding. Nothing could subscribe.
30	//
31	// It is also outbound network traffic from a product whose default build makes
32	// none, so the rules are strict and configuration cannot loosen them:
33	//
34	//   - Off unless ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL is set. No config file, no discovery,
35	//     no default endpoint. A URL has to be typed.
36	//   - brainNoEgressMode() wins. ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS silences
37	//     webhooks even with a URL configured, and the check happens here rather
38	//     than at each call site. A local-only promise one subsystem can opt out of
39	//     is not a promise.
40	//   - Fact text is withheld unless ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT says
41	//     otherwise, and that decision is made in newFactWebhookEvent so no caller
42	//     can forget it. The default payload is ids, kinds and taxonomy paths:
43	//     enough to trigger work, not enough to turn one env var into a feed of
44	//     everything the brain knows.
45	//   - Redirects are refused rather than followed. A webhook POST carries the
46	//     payload and its signature; following a 307 to somewhere else delivers
47	//     both to a host nobody configured. An endpoint that redirects is a
48	//     misconfiguration and is reported as one.
49	//   - Delivery never fails the command that triggered it. Recording a fact
50	//     succeeds or fails on its own terms; an unreachable endpoint is a warning
51	//     on stderr. The alternative is a brain that cannot write anything because
52	//     something unrelated is down.
53	
54	const (
55		webhookURLEnv         = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL"
56		webhookSecretEnv      = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET"
57		webhookIncludeTextEnv = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT"
58		webhookTimeoutEnv     = "ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT"
59	
60		// Delivery is synchronous and therefore on the critical path of every
61		// command that triggers it, so this is a latency budget rather than a
62		// generous ceiling. Two seconds is long enough for a local or same-region
63		// receiver and short enough that an unresponsive one does not make
64		// `remember` feel broken — it is called by agents, often.
65		//
66		// It cannot be made asynchronous by moving it to a goroutine: these are
67		// short-lived CLI processes, and a detached send is killed when the command
68		// returns, which is not "fire and forget" but "usually do not fire".
69		defaultWebhookTimeout = 2 * time.Second
70	)
71	
72	// webhookTimeout is the per-delivery deadline, overridable for a receiver that
73	// is legitimately slow.
74	func webhookTimeout() time.Duration {
75		raw := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookTimeoutEnv))
76		if raw == "" {
77			return defaultWebhookTimeout
78		}
79		parsed, err := time.ParseDuration(raw)
80		if err != nil || parsed <= 0 {
81			tui.Warnf(os.Stderr, "%s is not a positive duration; using %s", webhookTimeoutEnv, defaultWebhookTimeout)
82			return defaultWebhookTimeout
83		}
84		return parsed
85	}
86	
87	// The events that exist. Every name here is emitted by real code in this
88	// package; the list is deliberately not padded with events a consumer could
89	// subscribe to and never receive.
90	const (
91		WebhookFactRecorded   = "fact.recorded"
92		WebhookFactRetracted  = "fact.retracted"
93		WebhookBrainRefreshed = "brain.refreshed"
94		WebhookTest           = "webhook.test"
95	)
96	
97	// webhookCatalogue is the single list of what this brain sends and what each
98	// event means. `webhook events` prints it and the README quotes it, so neither
99	// can drift from the code; and because the descriptions live here rather than
100	// beside the command, a constant's only mention outside this file is a real
101	// emission — which is what TestEveryAdvertisedEventIsActuallyEmitted checks.
102	func webhookCatalogue() []struct{ Name, Description string } {
103		return []struct{ Name, Description string }{
104			{WebhookFactRecorded, "a durable fact was recorded (`remember`)"},
105			{WebhookFactRetracted, "a fact was marked no longer true (`facts retract`)"},
106			{WebhookBrainRefreshed, "the brain finished a refresh"},
107			{WebhookTest, "sent only by `webhook test`"},
108		}
109	}
110	
111	func webhookEventNames() []string {
112		names := make([]string, 0, 4)
113		for _, event := range webhookCatalogue() {
114			names = append(names, event.Name)
115		}
116		return names
117	}
118	
119	type webhookFact struct {
120		ID    string   `json:"id"`
121		Kind  string   `json:"kind,omitempty"`
122		Paths []string `json:"paths,omitempty"`
123		// Text is present only when ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT is set.
124		Text string `json:"text,omitempty"`
125	}
126	
127	type webhookEvent struct {
128		Event     string         `json:"event"`
129		Timestamp string         `json:"timestamp"`
130		Repo      string         `json:"repo,omitempty"`
131		Branch    string         `json:"branch,omitempty"`
132		Global    bool           `json:"global,omitempty"`
133		Fact      *webhookFact   `json:"fact,omitempty"`
134		Counts    map[string]int `json:"counts,omitempty"`
135	}
136	
137	// webhookRepoName is the repository's directory name, not its path. A consumer
138	// needs to tell two repos apart; it does not need to learn the layout of
139	// somebody's home directory.
140	func webhookRepoName(repoDir string) string {
141		repoDir = strings.TrimSpace(repoDir)
142		if repoDir == "" {
143			return ""
144		}
145		return filepath.Base(filepath.Clean(repoDir))
146	}
147	
148	// webhookRepoIdentity resolves the name every event for one repository reports.
149	//
150	// It must be one source for all of them. Call sites had drifted between the
151	// git-toplevel path and the configured repo root, which differ whenever a
152	// repository is reached through a symlink or from a subdirectory — so
153	// fact.recorded and fact.retracted could name the same physical repository
154	// differently, and a subscriber correlating by `repo` would see two.
155	//
156	// The git toplevel is the one that is stable under both, and it falls back to
157	// the configured root when git cannot answer.
158	func webhookRepoIdentity(ctx context.Context, opts Options) string {
159		if top, err := base.GitScalar(ctx, opts.Runner, opts.Env.RepoRoot, "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"); err == nil {
160			if name := webhookRepoName(strings.TrimSpace(top)); name != "" {
161				return name
162			}
163		}
164		return webhookRepoName(opts.Env.RepoRoot)
165	}
166	
167	// newFactWebhookEvent builds a fact event and is the ONLY place that decides
168	// whether fact text leaves the machine. Callers pass the whole record and get
169	// back a payload already redacted, so forgetting to redact is not something a
170	// call site can do.
171	func newFactWebhookEvent(name, repoName, branch string, record factRecord, now time.Time) webhookEvent {
172		fact := &webhookFact{ID: record.ID, Kind: record.Kind, Paths: record.Paths}
173		if base.EnvBool(webhookIncludeTextEnv) {
174			fact.Text = record.Text
175		}
176		return webhookEvent{
177			Event:     name,
178			Timestamp: now.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
179			Repo:      repoName,
180			Branch:    branch,
181			Fact:      fact,
182		}
183	}
184	
185	// webhookEndpoint resolves the configured endpoint, and explains itself when
186	// there is none — `webhook status` prints the reason, so a webhook that is off
187	// because of a typo is distinguishable from one that was never configured.
188	func webhookEndpoint() (endpoint string, ok bool, reason string) {
189		if base.BrainNoEgressMode() {
190			return "", false, "egress is disabled by " + base.NoEgressToggleName()
191		}
192		raw := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookURLEnv))
193		if raw == "" {
194			return "", false, webhookURLEnv + " is not set"
195		}
196		parsed, err := url.Parse(raw)
197		if err != nil {
198			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s is not a valid URL", webhookURLEnv)
199		}
200		// Scheme before host, deliberately: file:///tmp/x parses with an empty host,
201		// so checking the host first reports it as a malformed URL when the real
202		// objection — and the one the user needs to read — is the scheme.
203		// No filtering of loopback, link-local or private addresses, deliberately.
204		//
205		// SSRF is a confused-deputy problem: it matters when an attacker supplies a
206		// URL that a MORE privileged component fetches. This URL has exactly one
207		// source — an environment variable the operator sets — and no config file,
208		// discovery or remote input can reach it. Anyone who can set it already
209		// runs code as that user and does not need a webhook to reach the network.
210		//
211		// Blocking loopback would also break the primary local use: a receiver on
212		// 127.0.0.1 is the obvious way to consume these on a machine that is the
213		// point of a local-first tool.
214		//
215		// What would change this: if the endpoint ever became settable from a
216		// config file, a repository-local file, or anything a second party can
217		// write, it stops being operator input and the address filtering belongs
218		// back on the list.
219		if parsed.Scheme != "http" && parsed.Scheme != "https" {
220			// A file:// or unix:// "webhook" is not a webhook, and admitting one
221			// turns an environment variable into a write primitive.
222			scheme := parsed.Scheme
223			if scheme == "" {
224				scheme = "no scheme"
225			}
226			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s must be http or https, not %s", webhookURLEnv, scheme)
227		}
228		if parsed.Host == "" {
229			return "", false, fmt.Sprintf("%s has no host", webhookURLEnv)
230		}
231		return raw, true, ""
232	}
233	
234	// signWebhook returns the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the body, or "" when no secret is
235	// configured. Without it a receiver cannot tell a notification from this brain
236	// apart from a POST by anything else that learned the URL.
237	func signWebhook(body []byte) string {
238		secret := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv(webhookSecretEnv))
239		if secret == "" {
240			return ""
241		}
242		mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(secret))
243		mac.Write(body)
244		return hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
245	}
246	
247	// redactWebhookURL removes the endpoint from a transport error.
248	//
249	// For many receivers the URL IS the credential — a Slack or Discord incoming
250	// webhook is a secret path, and plenty of others carry a token in the query.
251	// http.Client.Do returns a *url.Error whose message embeds the whole thing, and
252	// this error is printed to stderr on every transient failure: into CI logs,
253	// agent transcripts and error monitoring. The host is enough to diagnose a
254	// delivery problem; the rest is a secret with no reason to be in a log.
255	func redactWebhookURL(err error) error {
256		var urlErr *url.Error
257		if !errors.As(err, &urlErr) {
258			return err
259		}
260		host := "the configured endpoint"
261		if parsed, parseErr := url.Parse(urlErr.URL); parseErr == nil && parsed.Host != "" {
262			host = parsed.Scheme + "://" + parsed.Host
263		}
264		// Rebuilt rather than string-replaced: the unwrapped cause carries the
265		// reason (timeout, connection refused, TLS failure) and does not contain
266		// the URL, so this keeps everything diagnostic and drops only the secret.
267		return fmt.Errorf("%s %s: %w", urlErr.Op, host, urlErr.Unwrap())
268	}
269	
270	// errWebhookRedirect is returned rather than followed. See the header comment:
271	// the payload and its signature must not be delivered to a host the user did
272	// not configure.
273	var errWebhookRedirect = errors.New("webhook endpoint redirected; point " + webhookURLEnv + " at the final URL instead")
274	
275	// Two bounds, deliberately: the client timeout covers the request and the
276	// context covers the whole operation. They are mutually redundant today —
277	// removing either alone leaves the other enforcing — so the test asserts the
278	// property (a stalled endpoint costs about the timeout and no more) rather than
279	// either mechanism. Removing both turns it red.
280	func newWebhookClient() *http.Client {
281		return &http.Client{
282			Timeout: webhookTimeout(),
283			CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
284				return errWebhookRedirect
285			},
286		}
287	}
288	
289	// emitWebhook delivers one event, or does nothing when webhooks are off. It
290	// returns an error so tests and `webhook test` can assert on delivery; the
291	// write paths use notifyWebhook instead and do not fail on it.
292	func emitWebhook(ctx context.Context, event webhookEvent) error {
293		endpoint, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint()
294		if !ok {
295			return nil // not configured is the normal case, not a failure
296		}
297		return deliverWebhook(ctx, endpoint, event)
298	}
299	
300	func deliverWebhook(ctx context.Context, endpoint string, event webhookEvent) error {
301		body, err := json.Marshal(event)
302		if err != nil {
303			return fmt.Errorf("encode webhook: %w", err)
304		}
305		if ctx == nil {
306			ctx = context.Background()
307		}
308		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, webhookTimeout())
309		defer cancel()
310	
311		request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
312		if err != nil {
313			return fmt.Errorf("build webhook request: %w", err)
314		}
315		request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
316		request.Header.Set("User-Agent", "entire-brain")
317		request.Header.Set("X-Entire-Event", event.Event)
318		if signature := signWebhook(body); signature != "" {
319			request.Header.Set("X-Entire-Signature-256", "sha256="+signature)
320		}
321	
322		response, err := newWebhookClient().Do(request)
323		if err != nil {
324			if errors.Is(err, errWebhookRedirect) {
325				return errWebhookRedirect
326			}
327			return fmt.Errorf("deliver webhook: %w", redactWebhookURL(err))
328		}
329		defer func() {
330			_, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4<<10))
331			_ = response.Body.Close()
332		}()
333		if response.StatusCode >= 400 {
334			return fmt.Errorf("webhook endpoint returned %s", response.Status)
335		}
336		return nil
337	}
338	
339	// notifyFactWebhook is what the fact write paths call.
340	//
341	// It checks whether webhooks are on BEFORE resolving anything, because
342	// resolving the repository identity shells out to git. Building the event
343	// eagerly and letting emitWebhook discard it put a subprocess on every
344	// `remember` and every `facts retract` for people who have never configured a
345	// webhook — which is the opposite of the promise that an unconfigured webhook
346	// costs nothing, on a path the rest of this file notes is called by agents,
347	// often.
348	func notifyFactWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, opts Options, event, branch string, record factRecord, now time.Time) {
349		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
350			return
351		}
352		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, newFactWebhookEvent(event, webhookRepoIdentity(ctx, opts), branch, record, now))
353	}
354	
355	// Global mutations belong to no repository, including the current checkout.
356	// Keep the same redaction and delivery policy without resolving a repo identity.
357	func notifyGlobalFactWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, event string, record factRecord, now time.Time) {
358		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
359			return
360		}
361		payload := newFactWebhookEvent(event, "", "", record, now)
362		payload.Global = true
363		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, payload)
364	}
365	
366	// notifyBrainWebhook is the same short-circuit for events that carry no fact.
367	func notifyBrainWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, opts Options, event string, now time.Time) {
368		if _, ok, _ := webhookEndpoint(); !ok {
369			return
370		}
371		notifyWebhook(ctx, errOut, webhookEvent{
372			Event:     event,
373			Timestamp: now.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339),
374			Repo:      webhookRepoIdentity(ctx, opts),
375		})
376	}
377	
378	// notifyWebhook is what the write paths call. It never returns an error,
379	// because no fact should fail to be recorded over a webhook — but it does
380	// block, for up to the timeout, and calling it "fire and forget" was wrong.
381	// A slow endpoint slows the command; ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT is how that
382	// is bounded.
383	func notifyWebhook(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer, event webhookEvent) {
384		if err := emitWebhook(ctx, event); err != nil && errOut != nil {
385			fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "warning: webhook %s not delivered: %v\n", event.Event, err)
386		}
387	}

+// documented in the README are deliberately absent: they are read at their point
+// of use and several resolve only by probing a server, which a read-only

Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.

- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.description:

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.
